Literary Analysis: Elements of Prose Fiction

A motif is a recurring image, object, or idea that develops a work's central concerns. A motif differs from a symbol in that a motif depends on repetition across the text, while a symbol can carry meaning in a single appearance.

An unreliable narrator is a narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt. Unreliability arises from limited knowledge, self-interest, or distorted judgement. Because the reader must reconstruct events the narrator misreports, an unreliable narrator forces active interpretation.

Free indirect discourse blends a character's idiom with third-person narration. The technique lets a novelist present a character's thoughts without quotation marks, so sympathy and irony can operate at the same time.

Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something a character does not. Dramatic irony generates suspense, because the reader anticipates a consequence the character cannot foresee.

Foreshadowing plants details that gain significance later in the narrative. Foreshadowing shapes expectation, and it makes a later reversal feel earned rather than arbitrary.

The climax is the point of greatest tension, where the central conflict reaches its decisive turn. Falling action follows the climax and resolves the consequences the turn has set in motion.
